description: We’re Team StarTrek—students using NASA data to solve real-world problems. We combine our skills in aerospace, science, and tech to turn big ideas into reality. Let's innovate.
summary: We developed “Flame in Freefall,” an SI-powered web dashboard that makes NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data easy to find, compare and interpret for fire safety in crewed exploration. Its built-in SI Research Guide lets users ask in plain language to rank studies for a Lunar Base, explain how electric fields mimic partial gravity (E-FIELD), or compare experiments side by side, and it summarizes each investigation’s findings. The dashboard ranks 25 PSI investigations by Fire Safety Relevance, Lunar and High-O₂ Relevance, and Partial-g and Modeling Value, and users can re-rank by habitat: ISS cabin, Lunar Base and rover (30% O₂ or more at 10.2 psi or less), Mars habitat, or spacesuit (up to 85% O₂ in ACME CFI-G). It also includes a 1g versus microgravity explainer, a 3D hardware and investigation network, a habitat flammability simulator with adjustable oxygen, pressure and airflow, a comparison table, and CSV, PDF and Word exports. It flags that PSI has no partial-gravity data yet and shows how existing results bound the Moon and Mars. It also links the research to Earth benefits, turning an overwhelming archive into clear answers that help make the next giant leap safer.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall is an interactive, AI-assisted web dashboard that makes NASA's microgravity combustion research easy to explore, compare and apply. It brings together 25 combustion and fire-safety investigations (PSI-10 to PSI-181) from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive. The data comes from experiments on the International Space Station, the Cygnus resupply spacecraft, the Space Shuttle and computational fluid dynamics models. The platform summarizes, ranks and simulates these findings so engineers, students and mission planners can see what they mean for crew safety on the Moon and Mars.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Enriched database. Each of the 25 studies is stored with technical metadata: burner and sample geometry, oxygen levels (13.5% to 85% O2), pressures (0.25 to 20 atm), ventilation speeds (0 to 65 cm/s), electric fields (0 to 10 kV) and diagnostic sensors. Studies are grouped into five research clusters: ACME Gaseous, Cool Flames, Solid Flammability, Soot and Smoke, and Fluid and Materials.

2. Ranking. Every study carries three 0-100 indicative scores: Fire Safety Relevance (crew-habitat fire safety), Lunar / High-O2 Applicability, and Partial-Gravity and Modeling Value. These scores were generated with AI assistance from each study's published PSI metadata. They are relative, comparison-oriented estimates meant to help users prioritize which studies to read first, not formally validated measurements. Users can rank by any score and filter by environment: ISS cabin, lunar base, pressurized rover, Mars habitat or spacesuit.

3. Physics visualizers. A split-screen view compares a buoyancy-dominated flame on Earth (1g) with a diffusion- and radiation-dominated spherical flame in microgravity, using live canvas models and annotated diagrams.

4. 3D hardware viewer. Rotatable Three.js models of four flight facilities: the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack, the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox, Cygnus (SAFFIRE) and the Space Shuttle (STDCE-1).

5. Knowledge graph. An interactive Vis.js network links the 25 studies through 25 engineering relationships, for example how the FLEX study (PSI-69) validates the OpenFOAM model (PSI-117).

6. Cabin fire hazard simulator. A parametric simulator, grounded in PSI-20, PSI-22, PSI-25, PSI-69 and PSI-159, lets users set oxygen (14% to 85%), airflow (0 to 45 cm/s) and cabin pressure (0.25 to 5.0 atm), or pick one of four mission presets, to see flame spread behavior and regime warnings.

7. AI Copilot (PSI Research Guide). The Copilot is powered by a large language model [Gemini API / Claude API]. Users ask questions in plain language, such as "Rank investigations for Lunar Base and Partial Gravity" or "Compare BASS-II and SAFFIRE-II". It answers from the platform's dataset and also operates the dashboard by filtering cards, re-ranking scores, switching 3D models and setting simulator sliders.

8. Comparison and export. Users can compare up to 4 studies side by side across 10 attributes, open a full telemetry dossier for any study with a link to its official NASA PSI record, and export PDF dossiers, Word briefs or CSV/Excel data.

KEY SCIENTIFIC INSIGHTS BUILT IN

- Turning off cabin ventilation does not put out fires in oxygen-enriched exploration atmospheres (26.5% to 34% O2), because burning polymers sustain themselves through radiative feedback (PSI-20).

- Gentle airflow (10 to 30 cm/s) in microgravity lets materials burn faster and at lower oxygen levels than on Earth (PSI-25, PSI-99).

- Electric fields can mimic lunar (0.16g) and Martian (0.38g) buoyancy, helping bound partial-gravity fire risk (PSI-22).

- Hot droplets that appear extinguished can burn as invisible cool flames (500 to 800 K) and reignite when disturbed (PSI-69, PSI-117).

- Smoke particles grow larger in microgravity and can evade older ionization alarms, so multi-wavelength optical sensors are needed (PSI-101, PSI-102).

- 85% oxygen tests bound spacesuit and airlock pre-breathe hazards (PSI-159).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Decades of NASA data become searchable and comparable in one place, so users can find the findings that matter for a given mission environment in seconds instead of reading dozens of technical reports. The intended impact is better-informed decisions on spacecraft materials, ventilation, smoke detection and fire response for crewed Moon and Mars missions. It also gives students and the public an accessible way to learn from NASA's open science data, and it points to Earth spin-offs of the research.

WHERE OUR DATA CAME FROM

All scientific data and context come from NASA's official resources listed on the challenge page: the PSI Data Repository (Combustion Science), NASA Combustion Science, the NASA ScienceCasts video "The Power of Studying Combustion on the ISS", and "A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science" (2015). Historical context came from the Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and 1997 Mir fire reports, and the fire-safety technology spin-offs (Fireman's Air Tanks, Fire Detector, Fire Attire). Each study in the dashboard links back to its official NASA PSI record.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Backend: Python with FastAPI

- Frontend: HTML5 Canvas, SVG, Three.js (3D viewer), Vis.js (knowledge graph)

- Development: VS Code, Windows PowerShell and Windows Terminal

- Version control: GitHub

- Hosting: Render.com

- AI: Gemini and Claude

- Hardware: standard laptops, no special hardware

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Rather than a static archive, it is an operating console. A conversational Copilot controls a scored database, a physics visualizer, a 3D hardware viewer, a knowledge graph and a hazard simulator together. The three mission-specific scores and the habitat filters turn raw experiments into answers about which research applies to a lunar base, a Mars habitat or a spacesuit. The knowledge graph also shows how experiments validate and cross-calibrate each other, which is hard to see in a plain list.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific grounding: studies, parameters and insights are tied to specific PSI investigations, and every study links back to its official NASA PSI record so users can verify the original data.

- Transparency about AI: the dataset enrichment, indicative scores and Copilot responses were produced with AI assistance. They are decision-support aids and should be checked against the official NASA records before any real engineering use.

- Mission relevance: scoring and filters reflect real exploration environments (ISS, lunar, Mars, spacesuit).

- Usability: keyboard search, one-click presets, and exports for Excel and Python users.

- Limitations: the scores and the hazard simulator are simplified, AI-assisted models. They are not official NASA safety standards and have not been independently validated.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

This project was developed using AI tools throughout. Gemini and Claude helped generate and refine the code, structure the dataset from NASA PSI sources, write the indicative scores, and draft documentation. Development was done in VS Code, with GitHub for version control, Render.com for deployment, and Windows PowerShell and Windows Terminal for running and deploying the project. The in-app PSI Research Guide Copilot uses a large language model at runtime. The science content comes from NASA's official PSI Data Repository and the resources listed on the challenge page, and every study links back to its official PSI record. The team directed the concept, reviewed the outputs and integrated the platform.
